ask.changes_what: Positive: fingerstick now, treat, and observe for recurrence (sulfonylurea/renal failure -> admit); negative: keep glucose check but move to cardiac/neurologic causes of the spell.
ask.contraindications: None; the history must never delay a point-of-care glucose in any patient with altered mental status, syncope or focal deficit.
ask.do_not_use_when: Never rely on symptom history alone in an obtunded, post-ictal or focally weak patient - measure glucose immediately.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypoglycemia with sulfonylurea, insulin overdose, renal failure or alcohol needs monitored admission and repeated glucose; persistent deficit after glucose correction is a stroke workup.
ask.how: Ask specifically about insulin or sulfonylurea use (drug, dose, timing of last dose), missed or delayed meals, alcohol, recent renal or hepatic decline, and prodromal autonomic symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) or neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, drowsiness, difficulty speaking, weakness). Confirm with a fingerstick glucose at the time of symptoms.
ask.negative_finding: No exposure to insulin or secretagogues and no critical illness, cortisol/hormone deficiency or alcohol makes drug-induced hypoglycemia unlikely, but a measured glucose is still required because neuroglycopenia can present without warning symptoms.
ask.pitfalls: Long-standing diabetes and beta-blockers blunt autonomic warning symptoms so neuroglycopenic presentation (confusion, focal deficit) may be the only clue; sulfonylurea hypoglycemia recurs for 24-72 h so a single corrected glucose is not the end of the episode.
ask.positive_finding: Insulin/secretagogue exposure plus a missed meal, alcohol or renal impairment and autonomic or neuroglycopenic prodrome makes hypoglycemia likely; Whipple's triad (symptoms, documented low glucose, resolution with glucose) confirms it.
ask.prerequisites: A collateral history when the patient is confused; the medication list including recently added sulfonylureas, insulin dose changes, or drugs that potentiate them.
ask.rationale: Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke and is rapidly reversible, so it's important to check for risk factors and symptoms.
ask.title: Hypoglycemia history: insulin/sulfonylurea use, missed meals, adrenergic or neuroglycopenic symptoms

examine.changes_what: Positive: activate stroke pathway/immediate imaging and time-critical reperfusion assessment. Negative: lowers probability but still image if dizziness, ataxia or visual symptoms.
examine.contraindications: None; if the patient cannot cooperate, observe spontaneous facial symmetry and limb movement instead.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a negative screen to exclude posterior-circulation stroke in a patient with acute dizziness, ataxia, diplopia or visual field loss; use HINTS/gait assessment and imaging pathways instead.
examine.escalation_warning: Any positive item with symptom onset within the reperfusion window is a time-critical emergency; do not delay activation for a glucose result unless hypoglycemia is confirmed and deficits resolve with correction.

evidence.citation: Goldstein LB, Simel DL. Is this patient having a stroke? JAMA. 2005;293(19):2391-2402.
evidence.population: Pooled studies of patients with suspected stroke evaluated with modern neuroimaging (RCE systematic review)
evidence.quote: LR of > or =1 finding = 5.5; 95% CI, 3.3-9.1 ... LR of 0 findings = 0.39; 95% CI, 0.25-0.61
evidence.reference_standard: Final diagnosis after neuroimaging and relevant laboratory tests
evidence.target_condition: Acute stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) among patients with neurologically relevant symptoms

evidence.citation: Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, Brott T, Broderick J. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378.
evidence.population: Convenience sample of 171 ED and neurology inpatients, 49 with stroke/TIA
evidence.quote: abnormality in any 1 of the 3 stroke scale items had a sensitivity of 66% and specificity of 87% in identifying a stroke patient.
evidence.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis of stroke or TIA
evidence.target_condition: Stroke or TIA (any 1 of 3 CPSS items abnormal, scored by physician)

evidence.citation: Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, Brott T, Broderick J. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378.
evidence.population: Same 171-patient convenience sample; subgroup with anterior circulation stroke
evidence.quote: The sensitivity was 88% for identification of patients with anterior circulation strokes.
evidence.reference_standard: Discharge diagnosis of stroke, anterior circulation
evidence.target_condition: Anterior circulation stroke (any 1 of 3 CPSS items abnormal)

examine.how: Ask the patient to smile or show teeth and look for asymmetric facial movement; have them close eyes and hold both arms out palms-up for 10 seconds, watching for one arm drifting down; ask them to repeat a simple sentence and listen for slurring, wrong words, or inability to speak. Any one abnormal item is a positive screen.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of all three findings lowers but does not exclude stroke (LR about 0.4); posterior-circulation strokes, which often present with dizziness or ataxia, are commonly missed by this screen (Kothari: 66% sensitivity overall vs 88% for anterior circulation).
examine.pitfalls: Bell palsy, old deficits, intoxication, hypoglycemia and seizure mimics all produce false positives; isolated vertigo, ataxia, visual field loss and neglect are not captured, so a negative screen must not stop a stroke work-up in a dizzy patient.
examine.positive_finding: Any new facial paresis, arm drift, or abnormal speech; in patients with neurologically relevant symptoms this raises the probability of stroke (pooled LR about 5.5).
examine.prerequisites: Patient awake enough to follow simple commands; check a fingerstick glucose alongside the screen. Note time last known well.
examine.rationale: A positive Cincinnati/FAST screen should trigger immediate stroke pathway activation and imaging.
examine.title: Facial droop, arm drift, abnormal speech (Cincinnati/FAST screen)

examine.changes_what: Cannot stand/walk unaided (grade 3): treat as central; stroke work-up regardless of HINTS. Walks unaided: lowers but does not remove need for HINTS; still image if other red flags.
examine.contraindications: Do not attempt to stand a hypotensive, actively vomiting or obtunded patient; use the sitting test instead.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not stand hypotensive, vomiting or obtunded patients; interpret with caution in patients with baseline gait impairment (neuropathy, parkinsonism, prior stroke, intoxication) where inability to walk is not new.
examine.escalation_warning: New inability to stand or walk unaided with acute vertigo is a central sign until proven otherwise, even with a normal CT and a peripheral-appearing HINTS; Carmona 2023 found truncal ataxia without nystagmus in 15% of acute-vertigo patients, mostly strokes.

evidence.citation: Tarnutzer AA, Gold D, Wang Z, et al. Impact of clinician training background and stroke location on bedside diagnostic test accuracy in the acute vestibular syndrome - a meta-analysis. Ann Neurol. 2023;94(2):295-308.
evidence.population: Pooled AVS cohorts (10 study cohorts, n=800; stroke and vestibular neuritis)
evidence.quote: Severe (grade 3) gait/truncal instability had high specificity 99.2% (95% CI = 97.8-100.0) but low sensitivity 35.8% (95% CI = 5.2-66.5).
evidence.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome (stroke or other central lesion) - severe (grade 3) gait/truncal instability

evidence.citation: Tarnutzer AA, Gold D, Wang Z, et al. Impact of clinician training background and stroke location on bedside diagnostic test accuracy in the acute vestibular syndrome - a meta-analysis. Ann Neurol. 2023;94(2):295-308.

evidence.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome - grade 2 or 3 gait/truncal instability

evidence.citation: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of a graded gait and truncal instability rating in acutely dizzy and ataxic patients. Cerebellum. 2024.

evidence.quote: Grade 2/3 GTI had moderate sensitivity (70.8% [95% confidence-interval (CI) = 59.3-82.3%]) and specificity (82.7 [71.6-93.8%]) for predicting a central cause
evidence.target_condition: Central cause of acute prolonged vertigo/imbalance - grade 2/3 graded gait/truncal instability (GTI)

evidence.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.
evidence.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (69 ischemic strokes vs 25 peripheral) at a stroke referral center
evidence.reference_standard: MRI (or CT) for stroke; normal MRI plus clinical follow-up for peripheral
evidence.target_condition: Ischemic stroke in AVS - severe truncal ataxia (cannot sit unassisted)

examine.how: With an assistant ready, ask the patient to sit unsupported, then stand, then walk a few metres. Grade truncal/gait instability: 0 = normal; 1 = mild sway but walks unaided; 2 = walks only with support/one-sided assistance; 3 = cannot stand or walk even with support (or cannot sit without arm support). If the patient cannot get up, note whether they can sit still unassisted.
examine.negative_finding: Walking unaided does not exclude posterior-circulation stroke: grade 3 instability is present in only about 36-44% of central AVS, so a patient who can walk still needs HINTS and imaging assessment when indicated.
examine.pitfalls: Peripheral vestibular neuritis causes unsteadiness (grade 1-2) that is easily over-called, especially in the elderly, the intoxicated or those with prior neuropathy; sedatives, Wernicke encephalopathy and alcohol withdrawal also produce ataxia. Grading systems differ (Lee 2006 vs Moon 2009), which changes sensitivity.
examine.positive_finding: Grade 3 instability (cannot stand or walk unaided) in acute vertigo is almost exclusively central - pooled specificity about 99% (LR+ high), and 0/25 peripheral patients in Kattah 2009. Grade 2-3 instability is more sensitive (71-81% pooled) but less specific (83%).
examine.prerequisites: Adequate blood pressure and no orthostatic symptoms; assistant present for fall prevention. Compare with baseline mobility in elderly or frail patients.
examine.rationale: Inability to stand or walk unaided suggests a central process and supports urgent stroke work-up.
examine.title: Ability to stand and walk unaided (truncal ataxia grade; inability = central marker)

examine.changes_what: Miosis + hypoventilation: give naloxone and support ventilation. Eye-movement signs + ataxia/confusion: IV thiamine now, before glucose. Gaze deviation: stroke pathway or EEG.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never withhold thiamine or naloxone because the eye or pupil findings are absent; both treatments are low-risk and the signs are insensitive.
examine.escalation_warning: Hypoventilation with miosis needs airway support and naloxone now; new gaze deviation or ophthalmoplegia with headache or focal deficits needs urgent neuroimaging.

evidence.citation: Harper CG, Giles M, Finlay-Jones R. Clinical signs in the Wernicke-Korsakoff complex: a retrospective analysis of 131 cases diagnosed at necropsy. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry. 1986;49(4):341-345.
evidence.population: 131 cases of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome diagnosed at necropsy, Western Australia, retrospective review of clinical records (80% undiagnosed in life)
evidence.quote: only 16% had the classical clinical triad and 19% had no documented clinical signs
evidence.target_condition: COMPOSITE: classic Wernicke triad (oculomotor abnormality + cerebellar ataxia + altered mental state) all documented antemortem, for necropsy-proven Wernicke-Korsakoff

evidence.citation: Caine D, Halliday GM, Kril JJ, Harper CG. Operational criteria for the classification of chronic alcoholics: identification of Wernicke's encephalopathy. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry. 1997;62(1):51-60.
evidence.population: 106 alcoholics screened from a large necropsy sample; criteria applied retrospectively to patient records by 3 independent raters; subgroup with Wernicke's plus hepatic encephalopathy
evidence.quote: Wernicke's encephalopathy was underrecognized only when occurring with hepatic encephalopathy (50% sensitivity)
evidence.target_condition: COMPOSITE: Caine operational criteria (2 of 4: dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar dysfunction, altered mental state/memory impairment) for neuropathologically confirmed Wernicke's encephalopathy co-occurring with hepatic encephalopathy

examine.how: Measure pupil size and reactivity in dim light, count respiratory rate for a full minute. Test horizontal and vertical pursuit and check for nystagmus, lateral rectus (VI) palsy or conjugate gaze palsy; note any forced gaze deviation at rest. Then test gait or heel-shin for ataxia and screen mental state and short-term recall.
examine.negative_finding: Normal pupils do not exclude opioid effect after mixed ingestions or hypoxia. The full Wernicke triad was documented in only 16% of necropsy-proven cases, so absence of eye signs must not withhold thiamine in at-risk patients.
examine.pitfalls: Miosis also follows pontine stroke, clonidine, organophosphates and cholinergic eye drops; mydriasis after hypoxic arrest can mask opioid miosis. Wernicke's without alcohol (bariatric surgery, hyperemesis, cancer) presents atypically; eye signs are frequently missed on record review.
examine.positive_finding: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory rate <=12 in an unresponsive patient points to opioid toxidrome and justifies naloxone. Nystagmus, VI palsy or gaze palsy plus ataxia or confusion in a malnourished or alcohol-using patient meets Caine criteria for Wernicke's and mandates immediate IV thiamine; forced conjugate gaze deviation suggests stroke or ongoing seizure.
examine.prerequisites: Pen light; ability to open the eyelids; record any recent opioid, sedative or eye-drop exposure and prior ocular surgery.
examine.rationale: Abnormal pupils or eye movements can indicate alternative diagnoses like toxidrome or Wernicke's, which require different urgent treatments.
examine.title: Pupils and eye movements: miosis with hypoventilation (opioid), ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus with ataxia (Wernicke), gaze deviation
